lessons.title: Review — three endings
lessons.gloss: review — three endings, and the arithmetic of what they just did to your vocabulary

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called What you've built until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Nothing new here. Say the three endings and their English partners before you look.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 3 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: Spanish, English, gender, roughly how many. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Three chapters. Between them they reach further than every vocabulary lesson in this book put together, and they will keep reaching for as long as you keep learning adjectives.

That is worth stating plainly, because it changes what you should expect from the rest of the book. A Spanish course is not mostly a list of words. A large part of it is a small number of rules that turn words you already own into words you can use — and you have just been handed three of the biggest.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: two kinds of ending

segments.text: The three are not the same kind of thing, and the difference matters:
-ción and -dad are decoders. They let you read a word you have never met. They have a fixed reach, because there are only so many English words with those endings.
-mente is a machine. It lets you build a word nobody taught you, from any adjective you hold. Its reach is whatever your adjective vocabulary turns out to be.
Both kinds are worth having, and neither is a substitute for the other. A decoder gets you through a page; a machine gets you through a sentence you have to say yourself.

segments.prompt: Give the three Spanish endings and their English partners.
Which of the three endings tell you the gender for free?

feedback.correct: Two endings, no gender decision ever.

segments.prompt: Which ending is a machine rather than a decoder, and why?
acceptedResponses: -mente, because you can build new words with it
-mente — it makes an adverb from any adjective

feedback.correct: A decoder reads; a machine builds.
feedback.incorrect: -mente. The other two let you read; this one lets you make.

segments.text: Three endings — name them. (-ción, -dad, -mente.) Which two are always feminine? (-ción and -dad.) Which one has no upper limit? (-mente.) Next: reading a sentence nobody taught you.
